A1.justification: Both PDFs describe StructTuning, despite the revised title. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated results.

before.justification: v1 reports original LongBench and MMedBench experiments, including component ablations, cross-language results, and knowledge-structure recall.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds Llama3-8B results, corpus-scaling experiments, extraction-model comparisons, and a QA-synthesis control.

M1.justification: The structure-construction component changes substantially: v1 uses few-shot Llama3-70B extraction, whereas v2 introduces a specialized Llama2-7B extractor distilled from teacher-generated examples. v2 also introduces recursive clustering for fragmented Japanese Wikipedia content. The downstream SCPT objectives and SSFT synthesis framework remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: The seven LongBench subsets and six-language MMedBench evaluation remain. v2 adds Japanese Wikipedia content to continual pre-training in the largest corpus and Wikipedia-derived training examples for the structure extractor. This extends training coverage beyond the earlier textbook-based injection setting; corpus-size increases alone are assessed under E3.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 adds reported comparisons with ChatDoctor, PMC-LLaMA, and MedAlpaca, previously only named, and removes MMedLM-7B. Appendices B.1 and B.4 add extractor comparators and random SFT synthesis. LongBench drops the unadapted CBQA and CPT-only controls. MMedLM2 remains under the InternLM2 '+MMed' label.

E3.justification: v2 adds 30.1M- and 132.6M-token training settings around the retained 76.1M setting, evaluates Llama3-8B, introduces an 8K random-QA control, and evaluates CoT-prompted OBQA recall. Section 3.1 also changes the stated segmentation from sentence level to paragraph level. Both F1 and recall remain evaluated despite their changed placement.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained English-training component ablation, v2 adds corpus-size sensitivity in Figure 7, extraction-quality and efficiency comparisons in Table A3, measured/projected cost analysis in Table A4, and a random-versus-structured QA synthesis control in Table A6. These test scalability, extractor choice, overhead, and whether extra data alone explains the gains.

E5.justification: v2 adds statistical estimation through fitting two quadratic functions of log corpus ratio in Equation 3. It provides no uncertainty estimates for these fits. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: New results include Llama3-8B MMedBench averages of 62.79 for the base model, 67.75 with MMed, and 65.36 with StructTuning; OBQA recall of 26.9; and scaling/extractor results. Table A6 adds random-SFT accuracy of 34.51 alongside retained SSFT* accuracy of 38.27. Retained Llama2/InternLM2 scores match v1; these additions do not establish version-to-version performance gains.

T1.justification: The SCPT probability formulations in Equations 1–2 are unchanged. v2 adds Equation 3, defining fitted scaling relationships and using mathematical extrapolation to predict corpus requirements and full-corpus enhancement. These are empirical relationships, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes obtaining about half MMedLM2's improvement using 0.3% of its corpus. v2 retains that claim but adds a headline claim of potential comparable improvement with 5% of training costs. This substantially extends the quantitative efficiency claim, although Section 4.2 identifies the underlying scaling predictions as empirically unverified.

C2.justification: v2 introduces interpretations involving OBQA attention drift and context limits, argues that approximate knowledge structures suffice, and extrapolates to 133% relative enhancement with full-corpus use. It also qualifies the scaling predictions as unverified and discusses preprocessing overhead. These materially extend the earlier explanations and scalability limitation.

D1.justification: v2 documents extractor training with 22K examples, batch size 128, learning rate 2e-5, and one epoch; expands corpus-construction instructions; reports runtime/cost information; and clarifies lexical exact-match evaluation. It reports code availability with a repository link instead of a future release. The earlier LLaMA-Factory disclosure and two few-shot examples are removed.

R1.justification: Section 2 replaces the conditional-language-modeling discussion with positioning against knowledge graphs and hierarchical retrieval, adding works such as K-BERT, DKPLM, RAPTOR, and content-aware indexing. v2 also credits Liu et al.'s structurization work for the specialized extractor. This substantively reframes the relationship to prior research beyond citation-format changes.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper and substantially reorganizes its narrative: LongBench becomes recall-led, F1 discussion moves to Appendix B.3, related work is rewritten, limitations move into the conclusion, and appendices are reorganized around additional experiments. These changes extend beyond wording corrections or added scientific content alone.

P2.justification: v2 adds the scaling plot, clustering diagram, and several analysis tables; splits the medical results into Tables 3–4; relocates and restructures LongBench tables; and converts the unchanged mindmap-recall Figure 7 into Table 2. It updates the extraction prompt display, removes two example figures, and changes the document template and headers.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens experimental support through the equal-sized random-QA control, extractor comparisons, and additional backbone evaluation, while improving implementation documentation and reporting code availability. The gain is limited by removing LongBench's unadapted control and elevating unverified scaling extrapolations into headline claims. The abstract's 5% training-cost claim also differs from the approximately 10% projection in the conclusion and Appendix B.2. These weaknesses temper the concrete improvements in validation and reproducibility.
